title: Are ten y minus three and ten times y minus three the same?
description: The letter-number y is replaced by two, ten, zero and seven in ten y minus three and in ten times the bracket y minus three, and the values are compared each time. They differ every time, so the expressions are not equal. Keeko's doubt is that the bracket changes nothing.
teaching_notes: One idea: a bracket changes the order of the operations, so ten y minus three and ten times the bracket y minus three take different values. Watch for students who think the bracket can be dropped without changing the value.

source: Replace y by 2, 10, 0 and 7 in 10y − 3 and in 10(y − 3), and
video_script.why: A learner sees how a bracket changes which operation is done first.
video_script.substitution: the book's two diagrams, with y replaced by two, ten, zero and seven in ten y minus three and in ten times the bracket y minus three
video_script.anchor: the two diagrams of the book, one for ten y minus three and one for ten times the bracket y minus three
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the bracket makes no difference because the same symbols are there. The bracket makes the subtraction come first, so the idea is broken with y as four.
video_script.payoff_line: Ten y minus three takes seventeen, ninety seven, minus three and sixty seven. Ten times the bracket takes minus ten, seventy, minus thirty and forty.

final_answer.value: 10y − 3 takes 17, 97, −3, 67 and 10(y − 3) takes −10, 70, −30, 40, so they are not equal
final_answer.spoken: ten y minus three and ten times the bracket y minus three are not equal

maths_rules: 10y - 3 means 3 less than 10 times y; 10(y - 3) means 10 times (3 less than y)
the values differ every time, so the expressions are not equal
Keeko test with y = 4: 10 x 4 - 3 = 37 and 10 x (4 - 3) = 10, which are not the same
video_script.design: The two diagrams stay on the board; each value of y is put into both expressions in turn and the two results are compared.

beats.on_screen: To find: the value of each expression for each y, and whether they are equal

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find both values for each y, and say if the expressions are equal.
<bookmark mark='two'/>Step one, y as two. Ten y minus three is twenty minus three, so seventeen. The bracket gives minus one, and ten times that is minus ten.
<bookmark mark='ten'/>Then y as ten. The first is ninety seven, and the second is ten times seven, which is seventy.
<bookmark mark='zero'/>Step two, y as zero. The first is minus three, and the second is ten times minus three, which is minus thirty.
<bookmark mark='seven'/>Then y as seven. The first is sixty seven, and the second is ten times four, which is forty.

beats.on_screen: Step 3, compare: 17 and −10, 97 and 70, −3 and −30, 67 and 40 all differ

marks.pairs: the four pairs of values are listed side by side
marks.differ: each pair is marked as different

narration: <bookmark mark='pairs'/>Step three, compare the four pairs of values.
<bookmark mark='differ'/>Every pair is different, so the two expressions are not equal.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 10y − 3 takes 17, 97, −3, 67 and 10(y − 3) takes −10, 70, −30, 40, so they are not equal
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Ten y minus three takes seventeen, ninety seven, minus three and sixty seven. Ten times the bracket takes minus ten, seventy, minus thirty and forty. Not equal.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the diagrams
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: 10y − 3 = 10(y − 3), struck out; the test y = 4 gives 37 and 10

marks.gap: 37 and 10 appear side by side and do not match

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the bracket changes nothing. Both expressions have a ten, a y and a three.
<bookmark mark='test'/>Try y as four.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>Ten y minus three is thirty seven, but ten times the bracket is only ten.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The bracket makes the subtraction come first, so it changes the value.
